title: Thinking as a Sikh today

segments.voice: Yesterday, honest citizenship: truthful living, higher than truth alone, carried into the form and the street. Your line was honest citizens. Did you do your civic duty, all of it? Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

What would the Gurus say about a phone that never stops buzzing? About a machine that can write a hymn? About medicine that can keep a body breathing long after the person seems gone? About a planet getting warmer? None of these questions existed when the hymns were sung. The Granth never mentions a screen. And yet Sikhs carry these questions into the gurdwara all the same, right past the shoes left at the door. So how do you think with an old book about a new world, without pretending it says what it doesn't? Today is about that skill, and the Sikh tools for it.
screen: `A PHONE, A MACHINE, A WARMING PLANET.` → `THE GRANTH NEVER MENTIONS A SCREEN.` → `AN OLD BOOK, A NEW WORLD.`

segments.voice: First, the Granth asks for thinking. In Raag Asa, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that when learning is truly reflected on, a person becomes a help to others. The word is vichar: reflection, turning a teaching over until it's yours. Reading isn't the end. Thinking it through is part of the practice. Second, a daily habit. Each day in the gurdwara, the Granth is opened and a hymn read from where it opens. That reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs bring whatever they're carrying to it, and then sit with what comes back. It's a way of letting an old Word speak into a new morning. Third, the community. When a new question touches the whole Sikh community, Sikh bodies such as the Akal Takht in Amritsar sometimes speak to it. Sikhs also talk, write and sometimes disagree, in homes and gurdwaras and online. Thinking as a Sikh today is done in company. Fourth, principle, not proof-text. There's no verse about phones. But there are threads you've met all year: remember the Name, work honestly, share, the Light in everyone, the good of all. Hold a new question up to those, and it starts to sort itself. Does this tool help me remember, or only forget? Does this choice treat everyone as carrying the same Light? That's what thinking as a Sikh can look like: old word, new question, and the patience to let them meet.
screen: `VICHAR: TURN THE TEACHING OVER.` · `THE HUKAMNAMA: AN ORDER EACH DAY.` · `THE COMMUNITY THINKS TOGETHER.` · `PRINCIPLE, NOT PROOF-TEXT.` · then, large: `OLD WORD, NEW QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one question to the Granth. Settle, and breathe. Let one real question come up, something the old world never faced: a choice about screens, money, work, a relative's care. Say it to yourself plainly. Then hold it up to one thread at a time. Breathe in: remembering. Breathe out: honest work. Breathe in: sharing. Breathe out: the good of all. Notice which thread tugs. If you'd like, look up today's hukamnama later and read it with your question in mind. The bell holds the time.
Thinking as a Sikh today. Vichar, reflection, bringing new questions to the old Word, with the community and the day's hukamnama. Today's word.
screen: `THINKING AS A SIKH TODAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: old word, new questions. Today, when a modern choice comes up, pause long enough to ask which old thread it pulls on, before you decide. Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras read a hukamnama, a hymn taken from where the Guru Granth Sahib opens, as the order of the day; Sikhs also discuss new questions together, and Sikh bodies such as the Akal Takht sometimes issue guidance.

notes: Please confirm Ang 356 for 'vidya vichari tan parupkari' and the paraphrase 'when learning is reflected on, a person becomes a help to others'. Day 1402 cited a different line on the same Ang.

The Akal Takht 'sometimes speaks' to new questions, and Sikhs 'sometimes disagree': kept general; please check framing.
